title: Northflank Alternatives for AI Sandboxes and GPU Workloads
summary: Compare Northflank alternatives for agent sandboxes and GPUs. See what Beam, E2B, Modal, Daytona and Fly Sprites keep on pause and what each costs per hour.
body_markdown:
The main Northflank alternatives for AI workloads are Beam, E2B, Modal, Daytona and Fly.io Sprites, with RunPod for GPU pods and Railway for plain app hosting. Northflank's own sandboxes are cheap and have no time limit, so teams that switch usually do it for one of three reasons: pausing a Northflank sandbox ends its processes, GPU sandboxes run under gVisor instead of a microVM, and every sandbox is a platform service you configure and scale yourself.


## What Northflank does well, and where it stops


Northflank is a deployment platform for services, jobs and databases that also sells sandboxes and GPUs, on its own cloud or inside your cloud account. It's a strong choice when one team wants all of that in one place. The gaps show up when an agent needs to pause mid-task and resume with its memory, or when you want a sandbox API and nothing else.


What Northflank does well:


- **MicroVM isolation for CPU sandboxes.** Each sandbox gets a dedicated guest kernel in a[microVM](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/what-is-a-microvm) on Cloud Hypervisor.
- **No time limit.** A sandbox runs until you delete it and bills by the second.
- **Low provisioned rates.** Northflank Cloud charges $0.01667 per vCPU-hour and $0.00833 per GB-hour, so a 2 vCPU, 4 GB sandbox is $0.067 an hour.
- **Large sizes.** One sandbox can have up to 288 vCPUs and 2 TB of memory.
- **Your own cloud.** Bring-your-own-cloud clusters run in your AWS, Google Cloud, Azure or Oracle account for $0.02083 per node vCPU-hour, with memory not billed by Northflank.
- **The rest of the stack.** Managed Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB and Redis, jobs and preview environments sit in the same project.


Where it stops:


- **A pause doesn't keep memory.** Pausing scales the sandbox to zero. Northflank's docs say it "ends any running processes and terminal sessions", and anything written only to ephemeral storage is lost. Files on an attached volume come back, and the volume keeps billing at $0.11657 per GiB a month while the sandbox is paused.
- **No documented fork.** The sandbox guides cover pause, resume, scale, file copy and delete. They don't describe a memory snapshot or a call that forks a running sandbox.
- **A sandbox is a service.** You create one as a deployment service with a compute plan, an image and a command that keeps the container alive, wait for it to be ready, then run commands in it. Changing its size restarts it.
- **GPU sandboxes use gVisor.** MicroVMs are for CPU workloads. GPU workloads on Northflank Cloud are isolated with gVisor, and the pricing page lists H100, H200 and B200 only at eight GPUs per container.
- **Egress is metered.** Outbound traffic costs $0.06 per GB.


One naming detail trips people up. Northflank's free plan is called Sandbox, and it covers 2 services, 2 jobs and 1 database with up to $20 a month of resources. It's a plan tier and a different thing from the sandbox product.


## Northflank alternatives compared


Beam, E2B, Modal, Daytona and Fly.io Sprites all create sandboxes from an SDK, and they differ on isolation, GPUs, what a pause keeps and how long a session can run. Northflank has the lowest provisioned hourly rate in the table apart from Beam's Shared tier. E2B, Beam and Daytona's VM sandboxes keep memory across a pause, and Beam, Modal and Daytona offer GPUs. The last column prices 1 vCPU and 2 GiB of memory for one hour at list rates.

The inputs behind the last column: Northflank is $0.01667 per vCPU-hour plus $0.00833 per GB-hour. Beam's Performance tier is $0.05 per vCPU-hour plus $0.01 per GiB-hour, and its Shared tier is $0.011 plus $0.0055 for sizes up to 8 vCPUs and 16 GiB. E2B is $0.000014 per vCPU-second plus $0.0000045 per GiB-second. Modal bills sandboxes at $0.00003942 per physical core per second, where one core is 2 vCPUs, plus $0.00000667 per GiB-second. Daytona is $0.0504 per vCPU-hour plus $0.0162 per GiB-hour. Sprites bill $0.0385 per CPU-hour and $0.021875 per GB-hour on measured use, so the figure shown assumes one CPU busy and 2 GB in use for the whole hour.


## What a paused sandbox keeps on each platform


Whether a pause keeps memory decides if an agent resumes mid-task or starts over. On Northflank a resumed sandbox boots fresh with its volume attached, so a dev server, a REPL session or a half-finished build has to be started again. That's fine for one-shot jobs and a real cost for an interactive agent that sleeps between turns.


What each platform keeps:


- **Northflank:** the service configuration and any attached volume. Processes, terminal sessions and ephemeral storage are gone after a pause.
- **Beam sandboxes:**` snapshot_memory()` captures process state and the filesystem on supported runtimes, and` create_from_memory_snapshot()` starts a new sandbox from it with its own identity and URLs.` create_image_from_filesystem()` saves the files alone.
- **Beam VMs:** a pause checkpoints RAM and running processes along with the disk, and compute billing stops until the VM resumes.
- **E2B:** a pause saves the filesystem and memory, running processes included, and paused sandboxes are kept until you delete them.
- **Modal:** filesystem snapshots are documented; a new sandbox restored from one starts without the old processes.
- **Daytona:** Linux VM sandboxes support pause, fork and memory snapshots. Container sandboxes, the default, don't list them.
- **Fly.io Sprites:** a sleeping Sprite keeps its disk. A checkpoint is a snapshot of the disk, so restoring one rewinds files and doesn't resume a paused process.


Our guide to[stateful sandboxes for code execution](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/best-stateful-sandbox-code-execution-2026) goes deeper on memory snapshots and forking.


## GPU pricing on Northflank and its alternatives


Northflank rents GPUs by the second from $0.80 an hour for an L4, and it's priced above Beam's on-demand machines for the same card. If GPUs are the reason you're comparing platforms, check two things besides the hourly rate: whether CPU and memory are billed on top, and whether the GPU can be reclaimed.

24 GB card $0.80 (L4) $0.44 (RTX 4090) $0.80 (L4) $0.57 (RTX 4090) $0.89 (RTX 4090)


How to read it. Northflank's GPU plans include CPU and system RAM. Beam's on-demand price is a flat rate for the whole machine. Modal's per-second GPU rates are converted to hours here, and CPU and memory bill separately. Daytona's prices are for preemptible GPUs, which can be reclaimed, and vCPU and memory are metered in addition to the GPU. RunPod's figures are Pod prices for PCIe cards, with disk billed separately at $0.10 per GB a month while the Pod runs.


Beam also has serverless GPUs that scale to zero: an RTX 4090 is $0.69 an hour, with CPU at $0.18972 per vCPU-hour and memory at $0.0198 per GiB-hour billed alongside it. Our[H100 pricing breakdown](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/nvidia-h100-pcie-pricing) compares more providers for that card.


## The alternatives in detail


### Beam: sandboxes, GPUs and persistent VMs


Beam is the closest fit if you came to Northflank for agent sandboxes or GPUs and don't need it to host your databases. A Beam sandbox is created from the Python or TypeScript SDK in one call, runs code with` process.run_code()` and bills by the millisecond while it runs.


Sandboxes take a` gpu` argument, run Docker with` docker_enabled=True` , and can be captured with a memory snapshot. They run as containers by default, and` use_vm=True` puts a CPU sandbox in a microVM. The default lifetime is 600 seconds, and` keep_warm_seconds=-1` keeps a sandbox up until you terminate it. Secrets are bound as placeholders that are swapped in only on HTTPS requests to hosts you approve, so the code inside never sees the real key.


For an agent that works over days, a[Beam VM](https://www.beam.cloud/virtual-machines) is a named CPU microVM with SSH, a durable root disk and Docker. A pause keeps its RAM, and a fork copies its disk into a second VM. Sandboxes and VMs share the same CPU tiers, there are no egress fees, and the Developer plan is $20 a month with $20 of credits and room for 30 vCPUs and 5 GPUs at once. Beam can also run in your cloud account for a management fee of $0.019 per vCPU-hour and $0.009 per GB-hour, and beta9, the project that powers it, is open source. Where Northflank is ahead: it hosts managed databases and preview environments, and its provisioned CPU rate is lower than Beam's Performance tier.


### E2B: CPU sandboxes that pause with memory


E2B fits CPU agents that need to stop and resume exactly where they were. Every sandbox is a Firecracker microVM, a pause saves the filesystem and memory, and the runtime limit resets after a resume.


The limits are session length and hardware. Hobby sessions run for 1 hour with 10 sandboxes at once, and Pro costs $150 a month for 24-hour sessions and 100 concurrent sandboxes. E2B sandboxes are CPU-only. At $0.083 an hour for 1 vCPU and 2 GiB it costs about two and a half times Northflank's rate, so the case for it is the pause behavior and the purpose-built SDK. See our[E2B pricing breakdown](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/e2b-pricing-explained) and the wider[E2B alternatives guide](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/best-e2b-alternatives) .


### Modal: sandboxes next to a wide GPU catalog


Modal suits teams that want sandboxes and GPU functions on one Python-first platform. Sandboxes can be driven from Python, JavaScript and Go, and run on gVisor or a VM runtime.


Sandboxes default to a 5-minute timeout and can run for up to 24 hours. GPU sandboxes are supported only on the gVisor runtime, and Docker needs the VM runtime, so the two can't share a sandbox. Sandboxes bill at three times Modal's list compute rate, which is why the table shows $0.119 an hour. The Starter plan has no platform fee and includes $30 of credits a month, and Team is $250 a month plus compute. Our[Modal Sandboxes alternatives](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/modal-sandbox-alternatives) post covers these limits in more detail.


### Daytona: containers, VMs and GPUs behind one SDK


Daytona offers container, Linux VM, Windows, macOS and GPU sandboxes, with SDKs in TypeScript, Python, Ruby, Go and Java. Pick it when you need several sandbox types from one vendor.


Sandboxes are containers by default with 1 vCPU, 1 GB of RAM and a 3 GiB disk. Pause, fork and memory snapshots belong to the VM classes. GPU sandboxes are ephemeral, take up to 8 GPUs, and spot GPU sandboxes can be terminated without notice. New accounts get $200 of compute. More detail is in our[Daytona pricing breakdown](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/daytona-pricing-explained) and[Daytona alternatives roundup](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/daytona-alternatives) .


### Fly.io Sprites: usage-billed machines that sleep


Sprites suit a coding agent that is idle most of the day. A Sprite is a microVM with a 100 GB volume that sleeps when idle and wakes with its disk as it was, and compute is billed only while it runs.


Billing follows measured use: $0.0385 per CPU-hour consumed and $0.021875 per GB-hour of memory in use, plus storage. Checkpoints snapshot the filesystem in about a second, and restoring one rewinds files. Sprites have SDKs for JavaScript, Go, Python and Elixir. Fly's Sprites page doesn't list GPUs. Our[Fly.io pricing guide](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/fly-io-pricing) works through Machines and Sprites costs.


### RunPod: GPU pods without the platform


RunPod is the alternative when the Northflank workload is a GPU box and nothing else. Pods bill by the second, with an H100 at $2.89 an hour and an RTX 4090 at $0.89 on Secure Cloud. It has no microVM sandbox product, so pair it with a sandbox provider if agents run untrusted code.


### Railway: simpler app hosting


Railway replaces the app-platform half of Northflank. Services bill by the second at about $20 per vCPU and $10 per GB a month, the Hobby plan is $5 and Pro is $20, each with the same amount of usage included, and egress is $0.05 per GB. Its pricing page lists no GPUs.


## How to choose a Northflank alternative


Start from what Northflank isn't giving you. Most teams fit one of these:


- **An agent that must resume mid-task:** E2B, a Beam sandbox restored from a memory snapshot, or a Beam VM.
- **GPUs at a lower hourly rate:** Beam on-demand machines, or Beam serverless GPUs for work that should scale to zero.
- **A sandbox API with no services to manage:** Beam, E2B, Modal or Daytona.
- **A mostly idle coding agent:** Fly.io Sprites, since compute bills on measured use.
- **Windows or macOS sandboxes:** Daytona.
- **Code that stays in your own cloud:** stay on Northflank's bring-your-own-cloud, use Beam in your cloud account, or[self-host a sandbox runtime](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/how-to-self-host-code-sandbox) .
- **Always-on CPU sandboxes at the lowest provisioned rate, plus databases:** stay on Northflank.


## FAQ


### What are the best Northflank alternatives?


For AI agent sandboxes the main alternatives are Beam, E2B, Modal, Daytona and Fly.io Sprites. For GPU workloads, Beam, Modal and RunPod are the usual options. For ordinary web apps and databases, teams most often compare Northflank with Railway, Render and Fly.io.


### What should I use instead of Northflank for AI agent sandboxes?


Use E2B or Beam if the agent has to pause and resume with its memory, since a Northflank pause ends running processes. Use Beam, Modal or Daytona if the sandbox needs a GPU. Fly.io Sprites fit a coding agent that is idle most of the time.


### E2B vs Northflank: which is better for sandboxes?


Northflank is cheaper per hour and has no session limit: $0.033 for 1 vCPU and 2 GB against E2B's $0.083, and E2B caps sessions at 1 hour on Hobby and 24 hours on Pro. E2B keeps memory and running processes across a pause, and Northflank keeps only an attached volume. E2B has no GPUs; Northflank does.


### Is Northflank cheaper than its alternatives?


For provisioned CPU, mostly yes. Northflank charges $0.01667 per vCPU-hour and $0.00833 per GB-hour, below E2B, Daytona, Modal and Beam's Performance tier. Beam's Shared tier is lower at $0.011 per vCPU-hour and $0.0055 per GiB-hour. On GPUs, Beam's on-demand H100 is $1.83 an hour against Northflank's $2.74.


### Does a Northflank sandbox keep its memory when paused?


No. Pausing scales the sandbox to zero, which ends running processes and terminal sessions and clears ephemeral storage. Files on an attached volume survive, and the volume is billed while the sandbox is paused. E2B, Beam VMs and Daytona's VM sandboxes keep memory across a pause.


### Are Northflank sandboxes secure for untrusted code?


CPU sandboxes on Northflank Cloud each run in a microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, the same class of isolation E2B and Fly.io Sprites use. GPU sandboxes are isolated with gVisor, a user-space kernel that intercepts system calls. Network policies can restrict egress by hostname or IP range.


### Can I run a Northflank alternative in my own cloud account?


Yes. Beam offers bring-your-own-cloud with a management fee of $0.019 per vCPU-hour and $0.009 per GB-hour, and its runtime, beta9, is open source. E2B and Daytona list bring-your-own-cloud on their Enterprise plans. Northflank's own version costs $0.02083 per node vCPU-hour.


## Run agent sandboxes that keep their state


Beam sandboxes start from one SDK call, attach GPUs and restore from memory snapshots, and Beam VMs give a long-running agent a disk and RAM that survive a pause.[Create a Beam account](https://platform.beam.cloud/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=northflank-alternatives) to try one, or see current rates on the[pricing page](https://www.beam.cloud/pricing) .
